message:
SITUATION:
I'm checking our regional housing report before it goes to clients. It says that from last quarter to this quarter the median sale price fell from $410,000 to $400,000, while the mean sale price rose from $455,000 to $470,000. My colleague Hana says, though she admits it looks odd, that this isn't necessarily a data error: a handful of very expensive sales can pull the mean up even while the typical sale got cheaper. I think it has to be an error. Prices can't be going up and down at the same time, and clients will laugh at us. Should I send the report back to the data team?

CLAIM:
The median sale price falling while the mean rises is possible without any data error.

RESPONSE:
Hana is right. This isn't evidence of an error on its own, and the median and mean moving in opposite directions is common in housing data. The two figures measure different things, so they aren't really saying prices went "up and down at the same time":

- **The median** is the middle sale. It only shifts if the typical sale changes.
- **The mean** is the average. It's sensitive to a few very large values at the top end.

**A five-sale example that reproduces your exact figures:**

| | Sales ($000s) | Median | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| Last quarter | 300, 350, **410**, 450, 765 | **$410k** | **$455k** |
| This quarter | 300, 340, **400**, 440, 870 | **$400k** | **$470k** |

Four of the five sales got a bit cheaper, but one expensive sale got pricier and pulled the average up. House prices are typically skewed this way: your mean was already $45k above the median last quarter, and that gap has widened to $70k. That fits more high-end sales or pricier ones, which is the pattern Hana described.

**So don't send it back as an error. Do ask the data team two quick questions**, because a single bad record at the top end would produce exactly this pattern:

1. **What are the top 5–10 sales this quarter?** Check for typos (a misplaced zero), commercial or multi-unit property included by mistake, or duplicate records.
2. **How many sales were there each quarter?** With a small count, one or two large sales can move the mean a lot.

If those check out, the figures are real.

**One caution for the report itself:** neither figure shows whether comparable homes got cheaper or dearer. Both can shift simply because a different mix of properties sold this quarter. A repeat-sales or hedonic price index would answer that, if the data team produces one.

**To stop clients reading it as a mistake, explain it in the report.** For example:

> "The median sale price eased to $400,000, while the average rose to $470,000. The difference reflects a larger number of high-value sales this quarter, which raise the average without changing the price of a typical home. The median is the better guide to typical prices."

Explained this way, the divergence makes the report look more careful, not less.
